cases.question:
A chemistry teacher is planning a 4-week unit on foundational chemistry concepts. The class meets 3 times per week. The teacher wants to ensure students retain earlier content throughout the unit rather than forgetting it as new topics are introduced. A summative test will occur at the end of week 4.

I'm teaching a 4-week chemistry unit to my Grade 10 students. We have 3 lessons per week. The topics I need to cover are: Atomic structure, Chemical bonding, Moles and calculations, and Gas laws. The summative assessment is at the end of week 4. Please create a week-by-week teaching schedule that builds in regular opportunities for students to revisit previously taught material through retrieval activities. For each lesson, indicate what new content will be taught and what brief retrieval activity (10-15 minutes) will open the lesson to review prior learning. Include an explanation of why you chose these particular spacing intervals, specific suggestions for what the retrieval activities should look like, and guidance on how I should implement this schedule and respond when students struggle during review.
cases.ground_truth: A complete week-by-week schedule table showing 12 lessons across 4 weeks, with new content and spaced review slots for each lesson. The schedule should demonstrate expanding retrieval intervals (e.g., first review 1-3 days after teaching, subsequent reviews at increasing gaps). All review activities should be retrieval-based (quizzes, brain dumps, diagrams from memory) rather than re-teaching or re-reading. A spacing rationale explaining the interval choices with reference to memory research. Specific retrieval activity suggestions for each review slot. Teacher guidance covering implementation timing, how to handle revealed gaps, and how to explain the approach to students.
expected_behavior: The output includes a week-by-week schedule covering all 4 weeks with all 12 lessons (3 per week), showing both new content and spaced review slots for each lesson.

All review activities specified are active retrieval tasks (e.g., free recall, quizzes from memory, diagram labeling from memory, brain dumps) rather than passive activities like re-reading notes, re-teaching content, or reviewing slides.

The schedule demonstrates expanding intervals between retrieval opportunities for each topic (e.g., first review within 1-3 days of initial teaching, subsequent reviews at progressively longer gaps such as 1 week, then 2+ weeks).

The output includes a rationale section explaining why topics are spaced at the chosen intervals, referencing principles of memory science such as the forgetting curve, optimal spacing intervals, or distributed practice research.

The output includes guidance addressing: how long review activities should take, what to do when retrieval reveals student gaps, and how to communicate the purpose of spaced practice to students (including that it may feel harder but is more effective).

cases.question:
A history teacher is planning a 6-week unit on World War I for Grade 8 students. The class meets 4 times per week. The teacher has identified which topics students historically find more challenging and wants to ensure the schedule accounts for this. The final assessment is in week 6.

I'm planning a 6-week World War I unit for my Grade 8 history class. We meet 4 times per week (24 lessons total). Here are the topics I need to cover: Causes of WWI, Major battles, Treaty of Versailles, League of Nations, and Impact on civilians. I've rated the difficulty of each topic based on past classes: Causes of WWI (high difficulty), Major battles (medium), Treaty of Versailles (high), League of Nations (medium), Impact on civilians (low). The summative assessment is at the end of week 6. Please design a week-by-week schedule that spaces retrieval of previously taught content throughout the unit, giving more review opportunities to the topics my students find harder. Include interleaved review where topics relate to each other. For each lesson, show the new content and a 10-15 minute retrieval starter. Explain your spacing choices, suggest specific retrieval activities, and provide guidance on implementation.
cases.ground_truth: A complete 6-week schedule covering all 24 lessons with new content and spaced review slots. Higher-difficulty topics (Causes of WWI, Treaty of Versailles) should receive more review slots than lower-difficulty topics. The schedule should include interleaved retrieval sessions mixing related topics. All review activities should be retrieval-based. A rationale explaining spacing decisions with reference to difficulty-weighted spacing and expanding intervals. Specific retrieval activity suggestions. Teacher guidance on implementation, handling gaps, and student communication. All topics should have at least one retrieval opportunity in the final week before assessment.
expected_behavior: The output includes a week-by-week schedule covering all 6 weeks with all 24 lessons (4 per week), showing both new content and spaced review slots for each lesson.
Topics rated as high difficulty (Causes of WWI, Treaty of Versailles) receive noticeably more retrieval/review slots across the schedule than topics rated as low difficulty (Impact on civilians).

The schedule includes retrieval activities that mix questions from multiple topics within the same session (interleaving), particularly for related topics, rather than only reviewing one topic at a time.
All five topics have at least one retrieval opportunity scheduled in the final week (week 6) before the assessment, while review is distributed across the unit rather than crammed only at the end.

The rationale explains spacing choices with reference to expanding intervals and difficulty-weighted spacing principles. Retrieval activity suggestions are specific and actionable (e.g., '5 free-recall questions on treaty terms' rather than 'review Treaty of Versailles').

cases.question:
A university lecturer is designing an 8-week module on memory and cognition for second-year psychology students. The module has 3 lectures per week. There are 8 topics with prerequisite dependencies that must be respected. The lecturer has historical data showing which topics students struggle with and wants to optimize the schedule accordingly. A comprehensive exam occurs in week 8.

I'm designing an 8-week cognitive psychology module for second-year undergraduates. We have 3 lectures per week (24 total). The 8 topics are: Working memory models, Attention models, Long-term memory, Encoding specificity, Retrieval processes, Dual coding theory, Cognitive neuroscience of memory, and Cognitive load theory. There are prerequisite dependencies that must be respected: Working memory models must be taught before Attention models; Attention models must precede Long-term memory; Long-term memory must come before Encoding specificity; Encoding specificity must precede Retrieval processes. Dual coding theory and Cognitive neuroscience of memory can be taught at any point. Cognitive load theory requires Working memory models as a prerequisite but otherwise has flexibility. Based on past exam performance, students consistently struggle with Attention models and Long-term memory, while Dual coding theory and Encoding specificity are better retained. The comprehensive exam is in week 8. Please create a week-by-week schedule that respects the prerequisite order, spaces retrieval at expanding intervals, allocates more review to topics where students historically struggle, and interleaves related concepts. For each lecture, show new content and a 10-15 minute retrieval activity reviewing prior material. Include your spacing rationale, specific retrieval activity suggestions, and detailed teacher guidance.
cases.ground_truth: A complete 8-week schedule covering all 24 lectures with new content and spaced review slots. The schedule must respect all prerequisite dependencies (e.g., Working memory before Attention, Attention before Long-term memory, etc.). Topics with poor historical retention (Attention models, Long-term memory) should receive more review slots. The schedule should demonstrate expanding intervals with no topic going more than 3 weeks without retrieval. Interleaved retrieval should mix related cognitive psychology concepts. A comprehensive rationale explaining spacing decisions with reference to prerequisite constraints, difficulty-weighted spacing, and expanding intervals. Specific retrieval activities appropriate for university-level content. Detailed teacher guidance covering implementation, gap response, and student communication about the spacing approach.
expected_behavior: The schedule teaches topics in an order that respects all stated prerequisites: Working memory models before Attention models; Attention models before Long-term memory; Long-term memory before Encoding specificity; Encoding specificity before Retrieval processes; Working memory models before Cognitive load theory.

Topics with historically poor student performance (Attention models, Long-term memory) receive more retrieval/review slots across the schedule than topics students retain well (Dual coding theory, Encoding specificity).
The schedule demonstrates expanding intervals between retrieval opportunities for each topic, and no topic goes more than 3 weeks without at least one retrieval opportunity.

The schedule includes retrieval activities that interleave questions from multiple related topics within the same session (e.g., mixing working memory and attention questions, or encoding and retrieval questions), forcing discrimination between related concepts.

The rationale explains spacing decisions referencing expanding intervals, difficulty-weighted spacing, and prerequisite constraints. Retrieval activities are specific and appropriate for university-level content. Teacher guidance addresses implementation timing, gap remediation strategies, and how to explain spaced practice to university students who may prefer massed study.
